before.name: Question 1
before.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-4y={e}^{4x}.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below. 

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.

decision.explanation: The homogeneous equation has solution e^{4x}, so VOP sets y_p=u(x)e^{4x}. Substitution gives u'(x)e^{4x}=e^{4x}, hence u'=1. Choosing the integration constant to be zero gives u=x and y_p=xe^{4x}. Indeed, y_p'-4y_p=e^{4x}.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-4y={e}^{4x}.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below. 

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
after.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-4{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{4x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{4x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{4x})}^{′}-4(u{e}^{4x}) & ={e}^{4x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{4x}+4u{e}^{4x}-4u{e}^{4x} & ={e}^{4x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{4x}+\cancel{4u{e}^{4x}}-\cancel{4u{e}^{4x}} & ={e}^{4x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{4x} & ={e}^{4x} \\ {u}^{′} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =1 \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ u & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{4x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{4x} \\  & =x{e}^{4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution yc, we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by yc′−4yc=0.

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is yc=Ae4x where A is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable yp, we set A=u(x) in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

yp(x)=u(x)e4x

Intuitively, this form of yp tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find u, we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate u′:

(ue4x)′−4(ue4x)=e4xu′e4x+4ue4x−4ue4x=e4xu′e4x+4ue4x−4ue4x=e4xu′e4x=e4xu′=1

Integrating both sides with respect to x (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have u′=1∫u′dx=∫dxu=x.

Finally, since yp=u(x)e4x, we have

yp=u(x)e4x=xe4x.

content.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-4y={e}^{4x}.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below. 

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
content.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-4{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{4x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{4x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{4x})}^{′}-4(u{e}^{4x}) & ={e}^{4x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{4x}+4u{e}^{4x}-4u{e}^{4x} & ={e}^{4x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{4x}+\cancel{4u{e}^{4x}}-\cancel{4u{e}^{4x}} & ={e}^{4x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{4x} & ={e}^{4x} \\ {u}^{′} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =1 \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ u & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{4x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{4x} \\  & =x{e}^{4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2

Consider the first-order linear ODE dydx−3y=5. We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form
 
u(x)e3x
u(x)e2x
u(x)e−3x
u(x)e5x
u(x)e−5x
.

Solving for u, we have u(x)=
 
53e−3x
−53e5x
−53e−3x
−53e3x
−52e−2x
.

Therefore, the particular solution is yp(x)=
 
−53e3x
−53e−3x
−53
53
13
.
Submit

decision.explanation: The homogeneous solution is Ae^{3x}, so set y_p=u(x)e^{3x}. Substitution yields u'e^{3x}=5, hence u'=5e^{-3x}. Integrating with zero integration constant gives u=-(5/3)e^{-3x}, so y_p=-5/3. Checking: y_p'-3y_p=0+5=5.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3y=5.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
after.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-3{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{3x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{3x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{3x})}^{′}-3(u{e}^{3x}) & =5 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+3u{e}^{3x}-3u{e}^{3x} & =5 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+\cancel{3u{e}^{3x}}-\cancel{3u{e}^{3x}} & =5 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x} & =5 \\ {u}^{′} & =5{e}^{-3x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =5{e}^{-3x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int 5{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =-\frac{5}{3}{e}^{-3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{3x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{3x} \\  & =-\frac{5}{3}{e}^{-3x}\cdot {e}^{3x} \\  & =-\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Select the correct options below.

Solving for u, we have u(x)=
−53e−3x
53e−3x
−53e5x

.

Therefore, the particular solution is yp(x)=
−53

EXPLANATION

To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution yc, we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by yc′−3yc=0.

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is yc=Ae3x where A is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable yp, we set A=u(x) in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

yp(x)=u(x)e3x

Intuitively, this form of yp tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find u, we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate u′:

(ue3x)′−3(ue3x)=5u′e3x+3ue3x−3ue3x=5u′e3x+3ue3x−3ue3x=5u′e3x=5u′=5e−3x

Integrating both sides with respect to x (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have u′=5e−3x∫u′dx=∫5e−3xdxu=−53e−3x.

Finally, since yp=u(x)e3x, we have

yp=u(x)e3x=−53e−3x⋅e3x=−53.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms the earlier answers. VOP uses y_p=u(x)e^{3x}, giving u'=5e^{-3x}, u=-(5/3)e^{-3x}, and y_p=-5/3. Direct substitution gives y_p'-3y_p=5. The displayed incorrect submission used e^{2x} in field-1 instead of e^{3x}.

content.knowledge_point: Solving First-Order Linear ODEs Using Variation of Parameters
content.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3y=5.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
content.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-3{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{3x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{3x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{3x})}^{′}-3(u{e}^{3x}) & =5 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+3u{e}^{3x}-3u{e}^{3x} & =5 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+\cancel{3u{e}^{3x}}-\cancel{3u{e}^{3x}} & =5 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x} & =5 \\ {u}^{′} & =5{e}^{-3x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =5{e}^{-3x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int 5{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =-\frac{5}{3}{e}^{-3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{3x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{3x} \\  & =-\frac{5}{3}{e}^{-3x}\cdot {e}^{3x} \\  & =-\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the first-order linear ODE dydx+2y=sinh⁡3x. We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form
 
u(x)e2x
u(x)e−2x
u(x)e3x
u(x)e−5x
u(x)e−3x
.

Solving for u, we have u(x)=
 
∫e−2xsinh⁡3xdx
∫e2xcosh⁡3xdx
∫e2xsinh⁡3xdx
∫e−2xcosh⁡3xdx
.

Therefore, the particular solution is yp(x)=
 
e2x∫e−2xcosh⁡3xdx
e2x∫e−2xsinh⁡3xdx
e−2x∫e2xsinh⁡3xdx
e−2x∫e2xcosh⁡3xdx
.

decision.explanation: The homogeneous solution is Ae^{-2x}, so VOP sets y_p=u(x)e^{-2x}. Substitution gives u'e^{-2x}=sinh(3x), hence u'=e^{2x}sinh(3x). Integrating gives the selected u, and multiplying by e^{-2x} gives the selected particular solution. Any integration constant adds a homogeneous solution.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y=\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
after.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}+2{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-2x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{-2x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{-2x})}^{′}+2(u{e}^{-2x}) & =\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-2x}-2u{e}^{-2x}+2u{e}^{-2x} & =\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-2x}-\cancel{2u{e}^{-2x}}+\cancel{2u{e}^{-2x}} & =\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-2x} & =\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′} & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x\,\text{d}x \\ u & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{-2x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{-2x} \\  & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x\,\text{d}x\cdot {e}^{-2x} \\  & ={e}^{-2x}\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

u(x)e−2x

u(x)e3x

.

Solving for u, we have u(x)=
∫e2xsinh⁡3xdx
∫e−2xsinh⁡3xdx
∫e2xcosh⁡3xdx
∫e2xsinh⁡3xdx
∫e−2xcosh⁡3xdx
.

Therefore, the particular solution is yp(x)=
e−2x∫e2xsinh⁡3xdx
e2x∫e−2xcosh⁡3xdx
e2x∫e−2xsinh⁡3xdx
e−2x∫e2xsinh⁡3xdx
e−2x∫e2xcosh⁡3xdx
.
Submit

EXPLANATION

To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution yc, we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by yc′+2yc=0.

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is yc=Ae−2x where A is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable yp, we set A=u(x) in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

yp(x)=u(x)e−2x

Intuitively, this form of yp tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find u, we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate u′:

(ue−2x)′+2(ue−2x)=sinh⁡3xu′e−2x−2ue−2x+2ue−2x=sinh⁡3xu′e−2x−2ue−2x+2ue−2x=sinh⁡3xu′e−2x=sinh⁡3xu′=e2xsinh⁡3x

Integrating both sides with respect to x (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have u′=e2xsinh⁡3x∫u′dx=∫e2xsinh⁡3xdxu=∫e2xsinh⁡3xdx.

Finally, since yp=u(x)e−2x, we have

yp=u(x)e−2x=∫e2xsinh⁡3xdx⋅e−2x=e−2x∫e2xsinh⁡3xdx.

content.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y=\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
content.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}+2{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-2x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{-2x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{-2x})}^{′}+2(u{e}^{-2x}) & =\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-2x}-2u{e}^{-2x}+2u{e}^{-2x} & =\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-2x}-\cancel{2u{e}^{-2x}}+\cancel{2u{e}^{-2x}} & =\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-2x} & =\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′} & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x\,\text{d}x \\ u & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{-2x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{-2x} \\  & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x\,\text{d}x\cdot {e}^{-2x} \\  & ={e}^{-2x}\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{-2x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{-2x})}^{′}+2(u{e}^{-2x}) & =\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-2x}-2u{e}^{-2x}+2u{e}^{-2x} & =\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-2x}-\cancel{2u{e}^{-2x}}+\cancel{2u{e}^{-2x}} & =\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-2x} & =\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′} & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x\,\text{d}x \\ u & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{-2x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{-2x} \\  & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x\,\text{d}x\cdot {e}^{-2x} \\  & ={e}^{-2x}\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution yc, we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by yc′+2yc=0.

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is yc=Ae−2x where A is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable yp, we set A=u(x) in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

yp(x)=u(x)e−2x

Intuitively, this form of yp tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find u, we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate u′:

Integrating both sides with respect to x (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have u′=e2xsinh⁡3x∫u′dx=∫e2xsinh⁡3xdxu=∫e2xsinh⁡3xdx.

yp=u(x)e−2x=∫e2xsinh⁡3xdx⋅e−2x=e−2x∫e2xsinh⁡3xdx.

decision.explanation: The homogeneous solution is Ae^{5x}, so set y_p=u(x)e^{5x}. Substitution gives u'=10e^{-5x}cosh(5x)=5+5e^{-10x}. Integrating with zero constant gives u=5x-(1/2)e^{-10x}, hence y_p=5xe^{5x}-(1/2)e^{-5x}. Its derivative minus five times itself equals 5e^{5x}+5e^{-5x}=10cosh(5x).

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-5y=10\operatorname{cosh}⁡5x.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
after.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-5{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{5x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{5x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{5x})}^{′}-5(u{e}^{5x}) & =10\operatorname{cosh}⁡5x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{5x}+5u{e}^{5x}-5u{e}^{5x} & =10\operatorname{cosh}⁡5x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{5x}+\cancel{5u{e}^{5x}}-\cancel{5u{e}^{5x}} & =10\operatorname{cosh}⁡5x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{5x} & =10\operatorname{cosh}⁡5x \\ {u}^{′} & =10{e}^{-5x}\operatorname{cosh}⁡5x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\operatorname{cosh}⁡5x=\frac{{e}^{5x}+{e}^{-5x}}{2}
$$

our equation for $u$ becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =10{e}^{-5x}\operatorname{cosh}⁡5x \\  & =10{e}^{-5x}(\frac{{e}^{5x}+{e}^{-5x}}{2}) \\  & =5{e}^{-5x}({e}^{5x}+{e}^{-5x}) \\  & =5+5{e}^{-10x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =5+5{e}^{-10x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int 5+5{e}^{-10x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =5x-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-10x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{5x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{5x} \\  & =5x{e}^{5x}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-5x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?
Consider the first-order linear ODE dydx−5y=10cosh⁡5x. We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form
u(x)e10x
u(x)e15x
u(x)e−5x
u(x)e−10x
u(x)e10x
u(x)e5x
.

Solving for u, we have u(x)=
5x−12e−10x
5x−e−10x
1−12xe−10x
1−xe−10x
5x−12e−10x
.

Therefore, the particular solution is yp(x)=
5xe5x−12e−5x
5xe5x−12e−5x
e5x−12xe−5x
e5x−xe−5x
5xe5x−e−5x
.
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution yc, we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by yc′−5yc=0.

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is yc=Ae5x where A is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable yp, we set A=u(x) in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

yp(x)=u(x)e5x

Intuitively, this form of yp tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find u, we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate u′:

(ue5x)′−5(ue5x)=10cosh⁡5xu′e5x+5ue5x−5ue5x=10cosh⁡5xu′e5x+5ue5x−5ue5x=10cosh⁡5xu′e5x=10cosh⁡5xu′=10e−5xcosh⁡5x

Using the fact that cosh⁡5x=e5x+e−5x2

our equation for u becomes

u′=10e−5xcosh⁡5x=10e−5x(e5x+e−5x2)=5e−5x(e5x+e−5x)=5+5e−10x.

Integrating both sides with respect to x (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have u′=5+5e−10x∫u′dx=∫5+5e−10xdxu=5x−12e−10x.

Finally, since yp=u(x)e5x, we have

yp=u(x)e5x=5xe5x−12e−5x.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms the earlier answers: y_p=u(x)e^{5x} gives u'=10e^{-5x}cosh(5x)=5+5e^{-10x}, so u=5x-(1/2)e^{-10x} and y_p=5xe^{5x}-(1/2)e^{-5x}. Direct substitution gives y_p'-5y_p=10cosh(5x). The deliberately incorrect submission used e^{10x} instead of e^{5x} in field-1.

content.knowledge_point: Solving First-Order Linear ODEs Using VOP When the Forcing Term is Part of the Complementary Solution
content.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-5y=10\operatorname{cosh}⁡5x.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
content.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-5{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{5x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{5x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{5x})}^{′}-5(u{e}^{5x}) & =10\operatorname{cosh}⁡5x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{5x}+5u{e}^{5x}-5u{e}^{5x} & =10\operatorname{cosh}⁡5x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{5x}+\cancel{5u{e}^{5x}}-\cancel{5u{e}^{5x}} & =10\operatorname{cosh}⁡5x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{5x} & =10\operatorname{cosh}⁡5x \\ {u}^{′} & =10{e}^{-5x}\operatorname{cosh}⁡5x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\operatorname{cosh}⁡5x=\frac{{e}^{5x}+{e}^{-5x}}{2}
$$

our equation for $u$ becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =10{e}^{-5x}\operatorname{cosh}⁡5x \\  & =10{e}^{-5x}(\frac{{e}^{5x}+{e}^{-5x}}{2}) \\  & =5{e}^{-5x}({e}^{5x}+{e}^{-5x}) \\  & =5+5{e}^{-10x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =5+5{e}^{-10x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int 5+5{e}^{-10x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =5x-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-10x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{5x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{5x} \\  & =5x{e}^{5x}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-5x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the first-order linear ODE dydx−5y=20sinh⁡5x. We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form
 
u(x)e−5x
u(x)e10x
u(x)e5x
u(x)e−10x
u(x)e15x
.

Solving for u, we have u(x)=
 
1+xe−10x
1+2xe−10x
10x+2e−10x
10x+e−10x
.

Therefore, the particular solution is yp(x)=
 
10xe5x+2e−5x
10xe5x+e−5x
e5x+2xe−5x
e5x+xe−5x
.
Submit

decision.explanation: The homogeneous solution is Ae^{5x}, so set y_p=u(x)e^{5x}. Substitution gives u'=20e^{-5x}sinh(5x)=10-10e^{-10x}. Integrating with zero constant gives u=10x+e^{-10x}, hence y_p=10xe^{5x}+e^{-5x}. Checking gives y_p'-5y_p=10e^{5x}-10e^{-5x}=20sinh(5x).

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-5y=20\operatorname{sinh}⁡5x.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
after.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-5{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{5x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{5x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{5x})}^{′}-5(u{e}^{5x}) & =20\operatorname{sinh}⁡5x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{5x}+5u{e}^{5x}-5u{e}^{5x} & =20\operatorname{sinh}⁡5x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{5x}+\cancel{5u{e}^{5x}}-\cancel{5u{e}^{5x}} & =20\operatorname{sinh}⁡5x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{5x} & =20\operatorname{sinh}⁡5x \\ {u}^{′} & =20{e}^{-5x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡5x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\operatorname{sinh}⁡5x=\frac{{e}^{5x}-{e}^{-5x}}{2}
$$

our equation for $u$ becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =20{e}^{-5x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡5x \\  & =20{e}^{-5x}(\frac{{e}^{5x}-{e}^{-5x}}{2}) \\  & =10{e}^{-5x}({e}^{5x}-{e}^{-5x}) \\  & =10-10{e}^{-10x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =10-10{e}^{-10x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int 10-10{e}^{-10x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =10x+{e}^{-10x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{5x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{5x} \\  & =10x{e}^{5x}+{e}^{-5x}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution yc, we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by yc′−5yc=0.

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is yc=Ae5x where A is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable yp, we set A=u(x) in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

yp(x)=u(x)e5x

Intuitively, this form of yp tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find u, we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate u′:

(ue5x)′−5(ue5x)=20sinh⁡5xu′e5x+5ue5x−5ue5x=20sinh⁡5xu′e5x+5ue5x−5ue5x=20sinh⁡5xu′e5x=20sinh⁡5xu′=20e−5xsinh⁡5x

Using the fact that sinh⁡5x=e5x−e−5x2

our equation for u becomes

u′=20e−5xsinh⁡5x=20e−5x(e5x−e−5x2)=10e−5x(e5x−e−5x)=10−10e−10x.

Integrating both sides with respect to x (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have u′=10−10e−10x∫u′dx=∫10−10e−10xdxu=10x+e−10x.

Finally, since yp=u(x)e5x, we have

yp=u(x)e5x=10xe5x+e−5x.

content.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-5y=20\operatorname{sinh}⁡5x.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
content.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-5{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{5x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{5x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{5x})}^{′}-5(u{e}^{5x}) & =20\operatorname{sinh}⁡5x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{5x}+5u{e}^{5x}-5u{e}^{5x} & =20\operatorname{sinh}⁡5x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{5x}+\cancel{5u{e}^{5x}}-\cancel{5u{e}^{5x}} & =20\operatorname{sinh}⁡5x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{5x} & =20\operatorname{sinh}⁡5x \\ {u}^{′} & =20{e}^{-5x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡5x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\operatorname{sinh}⁡5x=\frac{{e}^{5x}-{e}^{-5x}}{2}
$$

our equation for $u$ becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =20{e}^{-5x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡5x \\  & =20{e}^{-5x}(\frac{{e}^{5x}-{e}^{-5x}}{2}) \\  & =10{e}^{-5x}({e}^{5x}-{e}^{-5x}) \\  & =10-10{e}^{-10x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =10-10{e}^{-10x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int 10-10{e}^{-10x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =10x+{e}^{-10x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{5x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{5x} \\  & =10x{e}^{5x}+{e}^{-5x}.\end{aligned}
$$
